session_1758600551918_p5swp39: To what extent do you support or oppose upzoning policies that allow for higher density housing in traditionally single-family neighborhoods? Please explain your reasoning.
column3: I fully support upzoning policies.    The cities are overcrowded as it is.    There isn't really the ability to expand inside of the city.   The city also is traditionally more expensive, because it makes things easier.   You are now in a walkable area and have more access to the city life.    Single family neighborhoods are going to already be cheaper, and there is more area to build.   You don't have to build tons of highrises to make a difference.One high rise with 30 units inside is already giving 30 more options for affordable housing.   Its become a big need for us here.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What do you think are the most significant impacts, positive or negative, of increasing housing density in residential neighborhoods?
column3: The significant impacts may just be that the people who originally purchased these home in the area because it was outside of the city, less people, more quiet type of lifestyle, may have an influx of people in the neighborhood, however, I do not see this upzoning project's purpose to build a "new city".   I see putting several high rise buildings perhaps even spread out, just adding more affordable homes.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How do you think upzoning policies might affect housing affordability in urban areas?
column3: I think that if there are more options just outside of the city, it makes it easier for people to move a few miles out, and once the apartments inside of the urban areas start to empty, the rents will automatically come down creating a domino effect.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What impact do you believe increased housing density might have on neighborhood character and quality of life?
column3: I think that we need to think about all people's quality of life.    It's not going to hurt a neighborhood to add one or two larger buildings to accommodate more people.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How do you think upzoning might affect transportation systems and traffic congestion in cities?
column3: I would like to think that with upzoning would come more extensive public transportation options.    As someone who has traveled extensively, the USA has the WORST public transportation of any country that I have visited that was a developed country.     I think it's time we started addressing this.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What role do you believe local government should play in regulating housing development and density?
column3: I think that the local government should only really intervene when it comes to these new projects being purchased by real estate companies and large corporations.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How might environmental concerns factor into decisions about urban density and zoning?
column3: This is not of any concern to me at all

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What economic effects, both positive and negative, might result from changing zoning laws to allow more multi-family housing?
column3: I think that you would start seeing new coffee shops, yoga studios, and restaurants popping up.    I personally think thats amazing.    I know that some people prefer to have housing areas separate from business areas, but it doesn't mean that now there is a new mall opening next door.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How do you think the interests of current residents versus future residents should be balanced when making zoning decisions?
column3: I do think that the current residents should have some say in where those buildings will be build, ONLY if they are owners of the home, and ONLY is it is proven that these new buildings will reduce the value of their homes.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What role do you think social equity and access to opportunity play in discussions about zoning and housing policy?
column3: I think if we are discussing the "hood", and section 8, we will notice that the majority of those homes are inner city, and I do not think things will change for those people by building new homes.    Generally the only people concerned about the housing crisis are ones who pay their own rent

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What do you think are the main causes of Support for Upzoning, and how certain are you about these relationships? Please also indicate if these influences are positive (increasing) or negative (decreasing).
column3: Well, in the USA. most people who are working 40 hours a week, cannot afford to live on their own.    There is a huge disconnect between wages and rents.    I do not think the wages need to go up, I think the rents and cost of living need to go down.    Upzoning adds immediately more homes onto the market causing supply and demand to become more balanced.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Single-family neighborhoods have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: The only thing that would concern me is having enough access to good schooling for everyone.   How will the current school systems deal with more students, but the same amount of space.    Most of everything else for me is a very positive note

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Housing affordability have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: 100 percent.   The only reason for this is for affordable homes.    If you check zillow or other rental platforms, there are tons of homes for rent, but they arent always affordable in any way.   Lets add some competition and see those prices go down.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Affordable housing have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Again, I think the more homes that you have into the area, it just creates more competition. You may have 50 homes that are up for rent right now in the inner city, but they're $3, $4, $5, $6, $7,000. The majority of US citizens are not going to be able to afford that, especially on their own. The American dream used to be be 18, move out of your home. You can work and you can make something of yourself. Then you buy a house and blah, blah, blah. Now it's not accessible, so adding more homes adds competition and it's perfect.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Would small changes in More housing options outside the city lead to noticeable changes in Support for Upzoning, or would it take larger shifts? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: I personally think that if you have, you know, let's say you put four high-rises in a neighborhood. Most neighborhoods are fairly spread out. Four high-rises, you've got 30 homes there, that's 120 new affordable homes. I think that would have a significant impact on costs and it would make a difference.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Quality of life have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Other than traffic, I do not see how it would affect the quality of life, but when you start thinking about it, even if it adds 120 homes into a neighborhood, that's 120 cars. If you go onto any freeway interstate in the US, how long does it take for 120 cars to go? Seconds, maybe a minute. It's not going to make a big, big difference. So I do think that these skyrises are going to have to have parking inside of it, because that would be the only issue if it were a neighborhood that's predominantly street parking. I can see where that would be a cause of concern.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How would you describe the relationship between Public transportation and Support for Upzoning? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: As I've said previously, the United States is probably the worst when it comes to develop countries and their public transportation. I've been all over the world and it's embarrassing. It makes no sense that we do not have access. The more access you have to cities, the more access you have to getting around, it does recreate that American dream for people that you may not be able to afford a car and that's okay. You don't have to. You can just jump on the train and go to work wherever you want. It just allows people to make more money and allows the income distribution to be more fair.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does USA public transportation have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: USA public transportation needs to get it together and just actually make a system. It needs to force cities to make a system. By not having a good public transportation, it does limit people to what they can do. Not everybody can afford a car, not everybody can, you know, who wants to ride a bike for 10 miles? It rains. You know, you want, oh, let's walk. You can't walk in the US. It's not like other places. I think that you would be looking at it as a negative, but I think that it would force them to expand the public transportation, which is a positive.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Real estate companies have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: This is where I feel the government needs to come in and control this aspect. I think that the real estate companies, the large corporations, the entities like that that are literally using it for, I know it's a for-profit thing, but it cannot be for Airbnb's short-term housing. If you're going to build these big buildings, they need to be for long-term only. I would definitely not allow short-term rentals.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How would you describe the relationship between Multi-family housing and Support for Upzoning? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: Multifamily housing is great. A lot of different places in the world multifamily housing is how it happens. That's how they build generational wealth. They keep everyone together. Everybody works together. And it keeps the family together. The United States doesn't really do that. So I do not think it's going to affect anything in any way.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does New businesses have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: We're a capitalist country. New businesses have to come in. People have to be able to do that. That's what our country is all about. It's about business. It's about being able to make money. It's about being able to start your own thing. Guess what? Most people cannot afford to rent a shop in the inner city. Let's take Chicago. It's probably $10,000 in rent to rent a small shop. In the suburbs, maybe $2,000. Why would we limit this?

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Current residents' input have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: The current residents are absolutely, I would say more than likely, going to see this as a negative thing. People don't like change. They moved into their neighborhood for a reason, and I understand that fully, but guess what? You can move out. You can move out. Everybody else has been priced out. I'm not saying that it's a fair thing. What I'm saying is have a little empathy and sympathy for other people's situations.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Does Inner city housing have a positive or negative effect on Support for Upzoning, and how significant is this effect? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: If we're talking inner city housing as far as like urban hood section 8 Things like that you're not going to have to deal with that You need to make these buildings where section 8 is not allowed And I say this just because if you go into those neighborhoods, that's typically where you're going to find the crime Especially the violent crime in the large cities We don't want to expand that territory like gang violence things like that We don't want to expand their territory So no, I think it could be a problem if these new high-rises were to allow section 8 and government homes

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How would you describe the relationship between Cost of living and Support for Upzoning? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: There's a huge relationship. Cost of living has went up. It's, that is what it is. Gas, food prices, electricity, everything has went up. And with that, the housing costs as well, but the wages do not. However, the solutions to not increase the wages, every time there's a wage increase, there's also a shift and things costing more because now companies have to pay more for this and more for that. Stop raising the wages and just lower the cost of living.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: How would you describe the relationship between Access to good schooling and Support for Upzoning? Is it a strong or weak connection? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
column3: This is definitely another issue. Let's say you bring 120 new families into the neighborhood. With those 120, they all have two kids. Now you're at 240 children. That's a major influx into a school. I do feel that that's going to be one of the biggest things that's going to have to be taken care of. But I also feel like we need to have the ability to choose schools for children. Instead, let's say you're in the suburbs, and I'm a mom, and I have to leave at 6 AM to get to work. Their school doesn't open till 8 o'clock in the morning. But I'm supposed to send my child to the school next to my house. Why can't I send my child to a school next to my work? I think that those are bigger questions.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: What factors affect Upzoning policies, and which ones have the strongest influence? Please also indicate if these influences are positive (increasing) or negative (decreasing).
column3: For me the biggest strongest influence is going to be the housing market needing more competition. The more competition creates lower prices. Lower prices creates more affordability. It's not like we're gonna lower the wages. So once your home costs six, seven, eight hundred dollars less a month, guess what? Now you have that money to spend into the economy which boosts it all around.

session_1758600551918_p5swp39: Would small changes in Affordable homes lead to noticeable changes in Support for Upzoning, or would it take larger shifts? Does it have a positive effect (increasing it) or a negative effect (decreasing it)? How strong is this effect?
